newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. chief, Australian minister urge landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief, Australian minister urge landmines ban.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called on Thursday for negotiations to ban the production of nuclear bomb-making material and for a global ban on landmines, which he denounced as "weapons of terror".
In a speech to the Conference on Disarmament, Annan urged the 61-member state body to break the stalemate and reach consensus on its negotiating agenda for 1997.

His appeal was echoed by Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer, who announced his country was donating A$4 million ($3 million) for demining in Cambodia and Mozambique. Downer called mines "the great scourge of our day".

Britain's ambassador Sir Michael Weston presented a formal mandate for a committee of the Geneva conference to negotiate a global agreement to "ban totally the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel landmines".
As a first step, Britain would seek an agreement to ban exports by the end of the 1997 session in September, he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates there are some 120 million anti-personnel mines laid across the world, which kill or maim tens of thousands of civilians each year.
The United Nations-sponsored conference opened an eight-week session last week but lacks a formal negotiating agenda due to disagreement over how far to go in the field of nuclear weapons.

Japan appealed for negotiations to be started towards ending production of bomb-making fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium). The ultimate goal was a world free of nuclear weapons, Hisami Kurokochi added.
But Pakistan demanded a legally-binding pledge by all states to the objective of complete elimination of nuclear weapons.
Munir Akram, Pakistan's envoy, said negotiators should set a programme and timeframe for total disarmament. "In this context" his country was prepared to work on a fissile "cut-off" treaty.

Annan, on his first visit as U.N. chief to Geneva, said: "I add my voice to those who have expressed strong support for the urgent need to continue with the process of nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation."
"The possibility of nuclear accidents, illicit trafficking in nuclear materials and the threat of terrorism all underline the need to maintain progress in this area," he added.

He called on negotiators to build on the 1970 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), saying it laid down broad guidelines for further steps. The treaty, which aims to halt the spread of nuclear weapons, was indefinitely extended in 1995.
"One such step should be a convention banning the production of fissile material for nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices," Annan said.
Western countries favour pushing ahead with talks to halt production of fissile material and reach a global landmine ban.
But India and Pakistan are leading a non-aligned campaign to force the major powers to set up a committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a set timetable, diplomats say.
Only then would the non-aligned be ready to push ahead on fissile cut-off as part of a nuclear disarmament package.
However, the five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) refuse to negotiate total disarmament, preferring a step-by-step approach.

The U.N. chief said the rise in local and regional conflicts since the end of the Cold War had highlighted the issue of conventional weapons, including landmines, which kill tens of thousands of combatants and civilians each year.

"I welcome the growing movement in favour of national measures to curb the transfer and use of these weapons and the commitment of more and more states to negotiate an effective legally binding total ban on them," Annan said.
"These weapons have become weapons of terror."
